title: Tencent/LoopForge — Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
content:
English · 简体中文
Two ways to work · Quick start · SOPs · Features · Local · FAQ · Docs
loopforge-promo-v11-en.mp4
80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).
LoopForge is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to Main Bot in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an SOP (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in.
CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code do the work. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license.
Both paths track the same requirements, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.
The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.
Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships.
- Repeatable. Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs.
- Separated roles. Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat.
- Human in the loop. Approval gates where they matter. Read the report, approve, or send the work back to a chosen step.
- Observable and resumable. Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node.
- Your stack, your servers. CodeBuddy, Codex or Claude Code as executors. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime.
Install Git and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set LOOPFORGE_YES=1 to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access.
git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git
cd LoopForge
./start.sh
./start.sh pulls the GHCR release image pinned in compose.yaml without building locally (bash scripts/install.sh does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use ./start.sh logs, stop, restart or pull to manage it, and ./start.sh dev to build the checkout from source.
Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on 0.0.0.0:8090 by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP.
New accounts join the LoopForge demo project, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate:
- Switch to the demo project, open Templates, and open Platform check · script & approval.
- Click Run SOP. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step.
- Approve it from Needs review or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact.
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- Executors. Pick CodeBuddy, Codex or Claude Code beside the home composer, then a model. Each executor uses its own credentials from personal settings, and every SOP role can choose its executor independently (built-in roles default to CodeBuddy). Requirement clarification and AI notification summaries currently use CodeBuddy; scheduled assistant tasks run on the CLI the task selects. The Docker image ships CodeBuddy and Codex; Claude Code installs from npm on first use and is cached, so that first run requires npm access; native deployments need the CLI for the executor you choose.
- GitHub is optional. All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs.
- Delivering to a repository. Choose Connect GitHub in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project SOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR.
- Sandboxes. In the default Compose installation, SOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See deployment boundaries. Re-running the installer keeps your data.
- Accounts and access. New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false in .env turns that off). Read the account and access model before exposing it beyond your team.
- Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers. See Deployment.
- Hacking on LoopForge itself? bash scripts/dev.sh runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).
An SOP is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:
The SOP designer with the built-in bug-fix SOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.
Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in SOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.
A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.
A delivery we actually ran: four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The reusable acceptance case checks the files and results. See the validation record for scope and known gaps.
Built-in SOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.
Don't want to run a server? LoopForge Local brings the built-in delivery workflows straight into the coding assistant you already use:
# Run inside your target project, e.g. for Claude Code
npx -y loopforge-cli@latest install claude
Then run /start-devflow "<your request>" in Claude Code.
See the local guide for each host's entry point and editions for the differences. Source lives in local/. Local runs the built-in workflows today; exporting a platform SOP for standalone local execution is pla

report.summary: Tencent open-sources LoopForge, an MIT-licensed self-hosted workspace that wraps CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code in repeatable agent workflows with sandboxes, checkpoints and human approval gates.
report.background: Coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Tencent's own CodeBuddy are now capable of real work, but each run is essentially one-shot: the agent may skip planning, forget tests, review its own output or silently stop halfway. That is acceptable for demos and unacceptable for team delivery, where the same requirement must produce the same quality every time. Meanwhile, teams increasingly want agent orchestration to run on their own infrastructure, with their own model keys, repositories and access rules, rather than inside a vendor's cloud. LoopForge is Tencent's answer: an open-source (MIT) platform that separates planning, implementation, review and testing into distinct roles, chains them into versioned SOPs with scripts and human gates, and executes everything inside Docker sandboxes while driving third-party coding-agent CLIs as interchangeable executors.
key_points: An SOP (standard operating procedure) is the core abstraction: a DAG of nodes where each step declares its role, artifacts and dependencies, and the engine fires a step only when its inputs are ready. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs ship read-only as blueprints; teams copy, adapt and version them so every requirement follows the same stages and checks.

Roles are split rather than merged. Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools, so the agent that writes code is not the one grading it. A role can act as an SOP node or as a subagent inside chat.

Human gates and observability are first-class. Runs pause at approval steps where a person reads the report, approves, adds context, retries a failed node or sends work back upstream, and node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts are visible in one place so runs can be resumed rather than restarted.

Executors are pluggable. CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code can be chosen per conversation and independently per SOP role, using each user's own credentials, which keeps the orchestration layer separate from any single model vendor and lets teams mix cheap and strong models across stages.

Deployment is self-hosted and low-friction: clone, run ./start.sh, and Docker Compose brings up MySQL, the platform, built-in sandboxes and starter SOPs on port 8090, with optional GitHub OAuth for PR delivery. A separate LoopForge Local path installs the same workflows directly into Claude Code via npx.
report.impact: LoopForge signals that the competitive frontier for coding agents is shifting from raw model capability to delivery infrastructure: sandboxes, role separation, approval gates, audit trails and cost reporting. For the industry, it pushes orchestration toward open, self-hostable standards rather than closed clouds, and gives Chinese vendors like CodeBuddy a seat alongside Codex and Claude Code through an executor abstraction that discourages lock-in. For developers, it turns fragile one-shot prompting into something closer to CI/CD, with resumable runs and reviewable artifacts, though the Docker socket access model means it is built for trusted teams, not multi-tenant isolation. For regular users, the practical effect is steadier output: fewer half-finished tasks, more visible checkpoints, and a human deciding when work ships.
report.tools: Try LoopForge Local first with npx -y loopforge-cli@latest install claude inside a project, then /start-devflow in Claude Code. For the full platform, clone the GitHub repo and run ./start.sh with Docker. Worth comparing: OpenHands for sandboxed agent runtimes, Aider for lighter CLI pair programming, LangGraph or Temporal for building your own orchestration graphs, and Dagger for reproducible pipeline execution.
